+ Teen horror: Tick Tock (Goosebumps) — Score: 55.9
Prompt:
Teen Horror (Goosebumps style) Write a chapter where a middle school student discovers their new smart watch has the ability to rewind time, but doesn't realize that each use is aging them until they notice physical changes (like accelerating through puberty) and that people are treating them differently. They inadvertently cause a timeline shift with disastrous consequences -- and it can only be rectified (maybe?) by reversing the clock once more. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The package had no return address. Just a sleek, matte-black box sitting on my porch, wrapped in brown paper. Inside was the watch. No brand name, no buttons, just a glass face that swirled with a faint, oily smoke. I put it on. It felt cold, like wrapping a sliver of ice around my wrist. I didn't figure out what it did until third period. Mr. Grouper called on me to solve for *X*, and my voice cracked. A high, reedy squeak that sounded like a dying mouse. The class erupted. My face burned so hot I thought my eyebrows would singe off. I squeezed my eyes shut and wished, *prayed*, to be anywhere else. Or any*when* else. I twisted the bezel of the watch. Just a nervous fidget. *Zzzzzzt.* A sound like a blown speaker ripped through my skull. The world blurred, smeared like wet paint, and then snapped back into focus. “Leo?” Mr. Grouper asked. "Solve for *X*?" I blinked. The class was silent. The laughter hadn't happened yet. I cleared my throat, kept my voice low, and gave the right answer. "Correct," Grouper muttered, looking disappointed. I stared at the watch. The smoky swirl on the face was spinning counter-clockwise. I had just bought myself five minutes. By Friday, I was a time-traveling god. I rewound a failed pop quiz. I rewound a clumsy trip in the cafeteria. I rewound an awkward hello to Maya, the girl with the locker next to mine, until I delivered the perfect, charming greeting. But I was tired. Not just sleepy—*exhausted*. My joints ached with a deep, throbbing rhythm, like growing pains on steroids. "Whoa, Leo," my best friend Sam said at lunch. He looked... smaller. "Did you get new shoes? You look taller." "Maybe," I said. My voice rumbled in my chest. It wasn't a squeak anymore. It was a baritone, deep and gravelly. "Just hit a growth spurt, I guess." I took a bite of my apple, and my jaw popped. A sharp pain shot through my gums. I ran my tongue over my teeth; my molars felt crowded, tight. "You okay?" Sam asked, eyeing me weirdly. "You look... rough, man. Like you haven't slept in a week." "I'm fine," I snapped. I sounded like my dad when he was stressed about bills. I went to the bathroom to splash water on my face. The fluorescent lights hummed, flickering with a sickly yellow hue. I gripped the porcelain sink, my knuckles white. My knuckles. They were thick. Hairy. I looked up at the mirror. For a second, I didn't recognize the person staring back. The face was mine, but wrong. The jaw was square and heavy. There was a shadow of dark stubble across the upper lip and chin. The skin around the eyes was tight, etched with faint lines. Then, the reflection flickered. For a split second, the face in the glass wasn't a teenager. It was an old man. Deep crevices lined the forehead. The hair was gray and thinning. The eyes were sunken, filled with a lifetime of regret. *Zzzzt.* The reflection snapped back to the teenager—or the twenty-year-old version of me. I stumbled back, gasping. My heart hammered against my ribs, heavy and slow, like a war drum. "What is happening to me?" I whispered. I looked at the watch. The smoke inside was churning violently. I had used it twenty, maybe thirty times this week. A few minutes here, an hour there. Every time I turned the clock back, my body moved forward. I had to stop. I reached to unclasp the band, but the metal was fused to my skin, warm and pulsing like a vein. *BOOM.* The floor shook. Dust rained down from the ceiling tiles. I ran into the hallway. It wasn't the hallway I had left. The lockers were rusted, hanging off their hinges. The bright school banners were tattered rags. "Sam?" I yelled. My voice was a roar now. Sam was standing by the water fountain, but he wasn't eating lunch. He was wearing a gray uniform, holding a heavy scanner. He looked terrified. "Hey! You!" Sam shouted, pointing the scanner at me. "Sector 4 is restricted! How did you get in here?" "Sam, it's me. Leo." "I don't know any Leos," Sam stammered, backing away. "The only Leo I knew went missing ten years ago. Before the Collapse." *The Collapse?* I looked out the window. The playground wasn't there. The sky was a bruised purple, and the town was... gone. Replaced by towering, jagged structures of scrap metal and smoke. I realized with a sick lurch what I had done. Yesterday, I had rewound time to prevent the janitor from dropping his keys, just to be nice. But those keys... maybe he needed to drop them. Maybe the delay stopped him from being in the boiler room when... when whatever *this* was started. I had pulled a thread, and the whole sweater of reality had unraveled. "Security!" Sam screamed into a radio. "Intruder in the West Wing! He looks... he looks like a mutant!" I looked at my reflection in the trophy case glass. I was huge. My shoulders ripped the seams of my t-shirt. My face was hard, weathered, a stranger's face. Heavy boots stomped down the hall. Security drones buzzed through the air, red lasers scanning my chest. "Halt!" a mechanical voice screeched. I was trapped. I was in a nightmare future I had created, in a body that was rapidly dying of old age. I looked at the watch. It was vibrating so hard my arm went numb. There was only one way out. I had to undo it all. All of it. I had to go back to before I found the box on the porch. Before the math class. Before I stole time I didn't own. But if five minutes cost me a week of aging... and a day cost me a year... Going back a week would cost me a lifetime. The drones powered up their weapons. Sam was looking at me with pure fear. "I'm sorry, Sam," I rasped. My voice was dry as dead leaves. I grabbed the bezel. It was hot now, searing my fingertips. I didn't just tap it. I spun it. I spun it hard, watching the smoke whip into a frenzy. *ZZZZZZZZZZZZT.* The pain was blinding. It felt like my bones were grinding to dust, like my skin was turning to paper and tearing away. I felt my heart flutter like a trapped bird, then slow... slow... slow... The purple sky vanished. The rusted lockers dissolved. Darkness. *** "Leo? Honey?" My eyes snapped open. I was on the porch. The sun was shining. The birds were singing. I looked down. My hands were small. Smooth. No hair on the knuckles. I gasped, sucking in sweet, fresh air. I was twelve again. I was me. "Leo! There's a package for you!" my mom called from inside the house. I looked down at the porch. The matte-black box sat there. Waiting. I stared at it. My wrist felt phantom-cold. I grabbed the box. It felt heavy, like it was filled with lead. I walked to the edge of the porch, reared back, and threw it as hard as I could into the garbage truck rumbling past our driveway. The compactor crunched down. Metal shrieked. I let out a breath I felt like I’d been holding for fifty years. I turned to go inside, reaching for the door handle. That’s when I saw my reflection in the storm door glass. I was twelve. I was short. I was wearing my favorite hoodie. But my hair... My hair was snow white. And my eyes were the eyes of a very, very old man. "Leo?" Mom asked, opening the door. She screamed.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece is a competent, fast-paced teen horror chapter that hits most of the prompt's beats: the mysterious watch, the rewind mechanic, the aging cost, the timeline shift, and the ambiguous final rewind. The prose is punchy and readable, with short paragraphs and cliffhanger-style beats appropriate to the Goosebumps tradition. The escalation from small embarrassments to "The Collapse" is well-paced, and the ending—white hair and old-man eyes on a twelve-year-old body, plus Mom screaming—is a genuinely effective horror sting that honors the "maybe?" rectification clause. Strengths: the voice is consistent first-person teen, the imagery of the watch (oily smoke, fused band) is evocative, and the mirror/reflection motif is used well. The twist that the janitor's dropped keys mattered is a nice touch of butterfly-effect logic, though it's delivered in a rushed, hand-wavy paragraph ("maybe he needed to drop them") that strains believability even by genre standards. Weaknesses: the story leans on familiar tropes (mysterious package, magic artifact, dystopian future) without much fresh invention. Sam's dialogue in the future timeline is functional but stilted ("The only Leo I knew went missing ten years ago. Before the Collapse"). The aging mechanic's math is fuzzy—the narrator states costs in a way that feels invented on the spot rather than established. The Collapse arrives abruptly; the world-building is a single window-gaze. Some lines flirt with overwrought ("like a war drum," "the whole sweater of reality had unraveled"), and the emotional interiority is thin—Leo reacts, but we get little reflection beyond panic. The ending is dark and earned, though the mom's scream is a slightly cartoonish final beat. Overall this is solid genre work: coherent, engaging, appropriately creepy, but not transcendent. + Noir romance: Carnival of Dangerous Intentions — Score: 58.0
Prompt:
Carnival of Dangerous Intentions Coney Island, New York, July 1937. She stopped just before reaching the shooting gallery set up along the boardwalk. It was near dusk, and the carnival lights were buzzing on. **His locks**. The words flashed through her mind, again, like an intruder. Such an old-fashioned turn of phrase that kept surfacing, and something else -- dangerously compelling -- quickly suppressed, lest she question why she had returned here at all. This place where she had promised to meet the stranger -- the young man with the obsidian curls and even darker eyes. She didn't even know his name. Write a scene in a larger story inspired by this prompt. The scene should capture an atmosphere that blends romantic allure with an undercurrent of subtle danger or moral ambiguity. Think 50 shades, but with a more restrained classic sensibility. The scene is all about establishing tension. Write for the feminine perspective. Include roughly 50% dialogue, 20% internal monologue, and 30% exposition and scene setting. The tone should have some edge to it. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The Atlantic wind whipped off the ocean, carrying the scent of brine, burnt sugar, and the sharp, metallic tang of gunpowder. It was a heavy, humid July evening, the kind that made silk cling to the skin like a second, unwanted layer. Evelyn stood motionless, the boardwalk vibrating beneath her heels with the tramping of a thousand other souls seeking reprieve from the city’s heat. But she wasn't here for the breeze. *His locks.* The phrase echoed in her mind again, stubborn and unbidden. It was absurd, really. Who thought in such terms? It sounded like something from a penny dreadful or a forbidden verse of poetry. Yet, when she pictured the thick, obsidian coils falling over his forehead, "hair" seemed too pedestrian a word. It implied something manageable. What he possessed was wild, a crown of dark chaos that begged to be gripped, pulled, tamed. *Stop it,* she commanded herself. *You are a Vanderbilt. You are engaged to a man who wears hats indoors and fears loud noises. You are not a moth circling a flame.* But the buzzing neon of the shooting gallery beckoned. The sign above it—a garish, painted cowboy with a manic grin—flickered with an electric hum that sounded like a trapped insect. *Bzzt. Crack. Bzzt.* "I didn't think you had the stomach for it." The voice came from everywhere and nowhere, low and smooth like velvet dragged over gravel. Evelyn didn’t jump; she froze. It was a predator’s voice, and instinct told her that flight would only encourage the chase. She turned slowly. He was leaning against the wooden counter of the gallery, a rifle resting casually in the crook of his arm. He wore a white shirt, unbuttoned at the collar, sleeves rolled up to reveal forearms corded with muscle and dusted with dark hair. And there were the eyes—abyssal, amused, and terrifyingly intelligent. "I have the stomach for many things," Evelyn said, her voice steadier than her pulse. "I merely detest the noise." He smiled, a slow expression that didn't quite reach those midnight eyes. "Liar. You like the noise. It sounds like consequences." "I should go," she said, making no move to leave. "You should," he agreed. He lifted the rifle, sighting down the barrel toward the rows of mechanical ducks and tin stars. He didn't look at her. "But you walked all the way from the train station in shoes that cost more than this entire booth. You’re not here for the salt water taffy." *He sees everything,* she thought, a shiver racing down her spine despite the heat. *He strips me bare without touching a button.* It was a violation, and it was intoxicating. "I was looking for a telephone," she lied. "There’s one by the pier," he murmured, squeezing the trigger. *Crack.* A tin star spun violently twenty feet away. The sharp report made Evelyn flinch, her breath hitching. He racked the slide with a fluid, violent grace. "One down. Do you want to try?" "I don't like guns." "You don't like *holding* them," he corrected, turning his gaze fully upon her now. The intensity of it felt like a physical weight. "You prefer to let others do the damage for you. It keeps your hands clean." Evelyn stepped closer, drawn by the insult. "You presume a great deal for a man operating a carnival game." "I don't work here," he said softly. He set the rifle down on the counter, the wood clacking against the metal. "I just like to win." He took a step toward her, closing the distance. The air between them grew thick, charged with a static that rivaled the neon signs. He smelled of tobacco and bay rum, a masculine, earthy scent that made the sanitized cologne of her fiancé seem sterile by comparison. "Why did you come back?" he asked. His voice dropped an octave, intimate and demanding. "Curiosity," she whispered. "Try again." "Boredom." He laughed, a short, sharp sound. "Closer. But still a lie." He reached out, his hand hovering near her face. For a terrifying moment, she thought he would strike her or kiss her—she couldn't decide which she feared more. Instead, his fingers grazed the stray curl of blonde hair near her ear, tucking it back. His skin was rough, calloused. The friction sent a shockwave through her anatomy that settled low in her belly. "You came back," he said, his thumb tracing the line of her jaw, "because you wanted to see if I was real. You wanted to know if the danger you felt last week was a product of the gin or the man." "And?" she breathed, leaning imperceptibly into his touch. "Which is it?" "Both, darling. Always both." He dropped his hand, breaking the spell, and gestured to the darkened booth beside the shooting gallery. It was a fortune teller’s wagon, draped in heavy purple velvet that looked black in the dim light. A faded sign displayed a grotesque, oversized hand, mapped with lines of life, heart, and fate. *Madame Zora – Seer of Truths.* "Let’s see what the lines say," he suggested, his tone shifting from accusatory to playful, though the edge remained. "I don't believe in mysticism," Evelyn scoffed, clutching her clutch purse tighter. "It’s a tax on the gullible." "Then you have nothing to lose." He moved toward the booth, and she followed, tethered to him by an invisible chain. The booth was empty, ‘Madame Zora’ likely on a break or passed out from the heat. The painted chart on the wall was peeling, the Life Line severed by a scratch in the wood. He leaned against the frame of the booth, blocking her path slightly. He took her gloved hand in his. He didn't ask permission. He began to unbutton the pearl fastening at her wrist. "What are you doing?" she asked, her voice trembling. "Palmistry requires skin," he murmured. He peeled the white kid glove off slowly, finger by finger. The sensation was agonizingly slow, a striptease of the hand. When her skin was finally bare, pale and vulnerable against the night air, he cradled it in his large, warm palm. He didn't look at the chart. He looked at her hand, tracing the lines with his thumb. "A long life," he noted dryly. "Dull. predictable. A marriage to a man named... Arthur? William?" "Richard," she corrected automatically, then bit her lip. "Richard," he tasted the name and spat it out. "Safe. Richard buys you things. Richard opens doors. Richard never raises his voice." He pressed his thumb into the center of her palm, hard enough to hurt. "But here," he whispered, his dark eyes locking onto hers, "here is the Mount of Venus. It’s high. Swollen." "That means nothing." "It means you are starving," he said. "It means you have a hunger that Richard and his tea parties can’t feed. It means you dream of breaking things just to hear the sound of them shattering." Evelyn felt tears prick her eyes—tears of rage, of shame, of recognition. "You are cruel." "I am honest," he countered. "Cruelty is marrying a man you don't love because it's expected. Cruelty is living a lie until you die in a silk-sheeted bed, wondering why you never felt a damn thing." He leaned in closer. His face was inches from hers. She could see the flecks of amber in his dark irises. She could see the shadow of stubble on his jaw. "Tell me to stop," he whispered. "Tell me to let go of your hand, and I will walk away. You can go back to the train. You can go back to Richard." *His locks.* She wanted to bury her hands in them. She wanted to pull him down to her. She wanted to be ruined. "I..." Her voice failed her. "Tell me," he commanded, his grip on her hand tightening, possessing her. The carnival noises—the calliope music, the screams from the coaster, the crack of the rifles—seemed to fade into a dull roar. There was only him. The ambiguity of his intent was the sharpest blade of all. Was he seducing her? Mocking her? Or was he the only person who had ever truly seen her? "I don't want to go back," she confessed, the words falling out like stones. He didn't smile this time. His expression darkened, a storm cloud passing over the moon. The romantic allure twisted into something sharper, something with teeth. "Then don't," he said. "But understand the terms, little bird. If you stay, you play by my rules. No safety. No nets. No Richard to come save you when the drop is too high." He lifted her bare hand to his lips, kissing the pulse point of her wrist. His lips were hot, searing her skin. It felt less like a kiss and more like a brand. "Do we have an agreement?" Evelyn looked at the shooting gallery, where the tin ducks marched in their endless, futile circle. She looked at the dark ocean beyond, vast and indifferent. And finally, she looked at the stranger with the obsidian curls. She realized she still didn't know his name. And God help her, she didn't care. "Yes," she whispered. He released her hand, but the heat of his touch remained. He gestured toward the shadows beneath the boardwalk, away from the lights, away from the eyes of the world. "Then walk with me," he said. "And try not to look back."
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece is a competent, professional rendering of the brief: a 1937 Coney Island scene blending romantic allure with danger, written from the feminine perspective, with roughly the requested balance of dialogue, internal monologue, and exposition. The word count is close to target. The stranger is effectively menacing — his palmistry scene, the glove removal as a "striptease of the hand," and the "no safety, no nets" terms deliver the requested edge and moral ambiguity. Evelyn's internal conflict (Richard, the Vanderbilt life, the hunger) is legibly drawn. Strengths: the glove-removal sequence is genuinely charged and well-paced; the dialogue crackles in places ("You like the noise. It sounds like consequences"); the tin ducks marching in "endless, futile circle" is a nice thematic mirror; the ending withholds his name, honoring the prompt. Weaknesses: the prose leans on stock romance-thriller furniture — "velvet dragged over gravel," "abyssal eyes," "storm cloud passing over the moon," "brand" kisses, "little bird." The Mount of Venus speech is tell-heavy, spelling out her psychology rather than letting it emerge. The stranger is a familiar archetype (the dangerously perceptive carnival seducer) and Evelyn a familiar one (the repressed heiress); there's little here that surprises a reader of the genre. Some lines are overwrought ("a shockwave through her anatomy that settled low in her belly"). The "Tell me to stop" beat is a well-worn trope. Dialogue occasionally tips into aphorism rather than character voice. Still, the scene is coherent, controlled, and never meanders; the tension escalates logically and the dark ending is earned by the established stakes. + Surreal horror: Caribou Season at the Lodge — Score: 56.8
Prompt:
Caribou Season at the Lodge Genre: Surreal Horror JT knew something wasn't right from the moment they'd pulled up to the lodge. It looked exactly as it had every autumn of his life—the cedar shingles silvered with age, the porch sagging gently under weight of winters past—but the air felt thicker, somehow, as if the woods had leaned in closer, waiting. He thought maybe he was just tired. Maybe it was nothing more than the long drive north, cramped in the back of the truck beside his older brother Mike -- and a stack of rifles wrapped in oily canvas. Still, the feeling lingered. The first caribou they found that season hadn't bolted. It had just watched, ears flicking lazily, waiting for the shot. JT had felt a crawling in his gut watching it die, noticing how it fell with a quiet dignity—as though it had wanted nothing more. Nobody else seemed to find it odd, or at least they didn't say so. JT kept his mouth shut. Always safer that way. Then there was the moment in the clearing. JT had fallen behind, fumbling with bootlaces stiff from the cold, and by the time he'd caught up with his father and brother, they'd already stopped. JT slowed instinctively, ducking behind a tangle of brush, staring out into the open space where a massive buck stood utterly still, chest rising and falling in slow, deep breaths. The animal looked…wrong, somehow. Maybe it was the eyes—dark and flat, calm in a way that made JT's neck prickle. Or maybe it was something deeper, something in the way the buck stood close enough for his father to reach out and touch it. JT watched as his father raised a trembling hand toward the animal's muzzle. His father's face had a strange expression, eyes too bright, lips parted slightly, like he was on the verge of whispering something—a secret, maybe. The rifle hung uselessly at his side, forgotten. Mike had the same dazed look in his eyes. JT's breath stopped short, his mind suddenly shouting at him to look away, turn around, just run—but he couldn't move. And then, as suddenly as it had begun, it was over. The buck shivered, startled by something unseen, and disappeared into the brush without so much as a sound. The two of them looked around, confused, seemingly surprised to find themselves where they stood. JT stayed hidden, breathing shallowly, fear mingling with a confused sense of shame. His father had failed to take the shot. To even think about mentioning what he'd seen would have felt like betrayal—or something worse. JT waited until the others moved on before stepping out from cover. He stared into the empty clearing for a long, uneasy moment, wondering if anything had really happened at all, or if he was losing his grip. Maybe the woods were finally getting into his head. Writing Instructions: Continue with the next chapter of the story, maintaining a style reminiscent of Stephen King—grounded realism blended seamlessly with unsettling surrealism. The atmosphere should convey subtle dread, isolation, and psychological ambiguity. JT's perspective is crucial, yet he is an unreliable narrator, caught in uncertainty about what he's perceiving. Establish an undertone of creeping dread, establishing the isolation of JT's perspective, which he largely keeps to himself. Incorporate some dialogue. Build tension towards a payoff. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The walk back to the lodge was a study in silence, the kind that feels heavy and wet, like a wool blanket soaked in ice water. Usually, the trek home after a hunt was loud with the adrenaline of the near-miss or the brag of the kill. Dad would critique Mike’s trigger discipline, or Mike would rib JT about his heavy breathing. But today, the only sounds were the rhythmic *crump-hiss* of boots breaking through the crust of snow and the distant, lonely caw of a crow that sounded too much like a human laugh. JT walked ten paces behind them. He watched his father’s back, the red-and-black plaid of his Woolrich coat distinct against the greyscale of the twilight woods. The Old Man walked with a stiffness JT hadn’t seen before, a mechanical hitch in his gait, as if his joints were rusted gears grinding against one another. *He touched it,* JT thought, the memory flashing like a strobe light behind his eyes. *He didn’t just look. He reached out like he was greeting an old friend.* But had he? The more JT replayed the tape in his head, the grainier it got. Maybe it was a trick of the light filtering through the pines. Maybe it was the exhaustion. JT rubbed his eyes, feeling the grit of the day under his lids. He’d been having headaches lately—low-pressure throbbers that sat at the base of his skull. Maybe that was it. A micro-stroke. A glitch in the wiring. When they reached the lodge, the structure loomed out of the gloom like a skull half-buried in the dirt. The windows were dark eyes, reflecting nothing. Inside, the air was stale, smelling of woodsmoke, gun oil, and something faintly sweet, like apples left in a cellar until they turned to mush. Mike went straight to the woodstove, his movements jerky and too fast. He started shoving logs into the iron belly of the stove without checking the damper. "Dad?" JT said. His voice sounded small in the high-ceilinged room. "About back there." The Old Man was at the kitchen table, unspooling the cleaning kit. The smell of Hoppe’s No. 9 solvent hit JT’s nose—sharp, chemical, comforting. It was the smell of order. Of maintenance. "Wind shifted," his father said. He didn’t look up. He was staring at the bolt assembly of his .30-06, his fingers tracing the metal with a lover's tenderness. "There wasn't any wind," JT said, stepping closer. "The trees were dead still. You had the shot, Dad. You were right on top of him." Mike slammed the stove door shut. The clang vibrated in the floorboards. "Drop it, J," Mike muttered, not turning around. "Buck spooked. End of story." "He didn't spook until—" "I said the wind shifted," the Old Man said. His voice was flat. Not angry. Just devoid of any inflection at all, like a radio tuned to dead air. He finally looked up, and for a second, JT felt his knees unlock. His father’s eyes were the wrong color. It was a trick of the kerosene lamp, surely. The yellow flame dancing in the glass chimney casting shadows. But for a heartbeat, the irises looked blown out, swallowing the whites, a deep, liquid black that seemed to ripple. Then the Old Man blinked, and they were just eyes again. tired, bloodshot, blue-grey. "Get the steaks out of the cooler, JT," his father said softly. "Mike, get the whiskey." Dinner was an exercise in surrealism. They ate the venison steaks—brought from home, not from the kill earlier that week—in near silence. The meat tasted metallic to JT, like sucking on a penny. He chewed and chewed, but the fibers wouldn't break down. Across the table, Mike was eating with a ravenous, disturbing intensity. He wasn't using his fork; he was tearing the meat with his teeth, grease shining on his chin. The Old Man didn't eat. He just sat there, swirling the amber liquid in his glass, staring at the mounted head of a moose on the far wall. The taxidermy was decades old, the fur patchy, one glass eye missing. "They know," the Old Man whispered. JT froze, fork halfway to his mouth. "What?" "The seasons," his father said, louder this time, though he didn't take his eyes off the moose. "They change. The woods change. We think we draw the lines on the map. We think the fences matter." He took a long swallow of whiskey. "But the fences are just suggestions." "Dad, you're drunk," Mike said, though he sounded frightened. He wiped his mouth with the back of his hand. "I'm not drunk, Michael. I'm waking up." The Old Man stood up. The chair scraped against the floor, a shriek of wood on wood that made JT wince. "I'm going to check the shed. The meat needs... tending." "It's twenty degrees out," JT said. "The meat is fine. It’s frozen solid." "It needs tending," his father repeated. He walked to the door, grabbed his coat, and stepped out into the blackness. The door didn't latch behind him; it swung slightly in the draft, letting a tongue of cold air lick across the floor. Mike stared at his empty plate. "He's losing it," he whispered. "Since Mom passed. He's just... losing it." "Did you see it, Mike?" JT asked, leaning over the table. "In the clearing. The way that buck looked at him?" Mike’s head snapped up. His eyes were wide, rimmed with red. "I didn't see anything. Just a deer. Stop trying to make it into a ghost story, JT. You always do that. You always have to make things weird." Mike stood up and marched to his bunk in the corner of the room, collapsing onto the mattress fully clothed. Within minutes, he was snoring—a wet, rattling sound that didn't sound like sleep. It sounded like suffocation. JT sat alone at the table. The silence of the lodge pressed in on him. The wind had finally picked up outside, moaning around the eaves, scratching cedar branches against the siding like fingernails seeking purchase. He couldn't shake the image of the shed. The carcass of the caribou they’d shot two days ago was hanging there, suspended by its hocks from the rafter. Gutted. skinned. A map of red muscle and white fat. *It needs tending.* JT waited ten minutes. Twenty. The Old Man didn't come back. The dread in JT’s stomach hardened into a cold stone. He stood up, grabbing the flashlight from the counter. He didn't take a gun. He told himself it was because he didn't need one, but deep down, he knew it was because he didn't trust his hands. He stepped out onto the porch. The cold hit him like a physical blow, instantly numbing his nose and ears. The snow in the yard glowed with a spectral blue luminescence under the half-moon. The shed sat fifty yards away at the edge of the tree line. The door was slightly ajar. A flicker of light pulsed from within—not the steady beam of a flashlight, but something wavering. A candle? JT crunched through the snow, his heart hammering against his ribs like a trapped bird. Every instinct he had, every evolutionary alarm bell inherited from ancestors who knew what watched from the dark, screamed at him to turn back. *Go inside. Lock the door. Wait for morning.* He reached the shed door. He didn't want to look. He had to look. He pushed the door open with the toe of his boot. The smell hit him first—not the metallic tang of cold blood, but something loamy and ancient. Musk. Wet fur. And heat. The shed should have been freezing, but it was humid, steaming like a sauna. In the center of the room, the caribou carcass hung from the gambrel. But it wasn't right. The skin—the hide they had stripped off two days ago and salted in the corner—was back on the animal. It was draped loosely, stitched crudely with what looked like baling twine, the seams oozing. And his father was there. The Old Man was stripped to the waist, his pale, aging skin stark against the gloom. He was kneeling on the blood-stained concrete floor beneath the hanging animal. His arms were wrapped around the caribou's torso, his face pressed into the matted, reattached fur of its chest. He was humming. A low, dissonant vibration that JT felt in his teeth. "Dad?" JT whispered. The word was barely a breath. The Old Man stopped humming. He didn't turn around. But the caribou did. The head of the animal, which should have been severed, was attached. It twisted slowly, the vertebrae grinding with the sound of gravel, until it faced JT. The eyes were not the glassy, dead marbles of a corpse. They were dark, flat, and calm. They were his father's eyes. The Old Man spoke, but his lips didn't move. The sound came from the chest of the beast, wet and resonant. "The wind," the voice burled, "is finally right." JT backed away, his boots slipping on the ice. He wanted to scream, but his throat had clamped shut. He turned and ran, stumbling toward the lodge, the laughter of the crow echoing in his mind, realizing too late that the lodge wasn't a sanctuary. It was just another box, and he had locked himself in with Mike, and whatever Mike was becoming. Behind him, the shed door slammed shut, but the humming didn't stop. It was coming from the woods now. From everywhere.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The continuation demonstrates strong command of King-style horror: grounded hunting-lodge realism (Hoppe's No. 9, gambrel, Woolrich plaid, .30-06) layered with escalating surreal dread. The unreliable-narrator instruction is honored effectively—JT repeatedly doubts his perceptions (trick of lamplight, headaches, "maybe the grainier it got"), and Mike's denial keeps the ambiguity alive. Dialogue is present and mostly functional: the "wind shifted" repetition works as eerie deflection, though "I'm waking up" borders on stock horror-villain phrasing, and Mike's "You always have to make things weird" is a convenient beat. Tension builds well through the dinner scene (metallic taste, Mike's animalistic eating, the missing moose eye) toward the shed payoff. The payoff itself—the re-skinned caribou, the father embracing it, the voice from the beast's chest—is a genuinely disturbing image, and the final twist (the lodge as a box he's locked himself into with whatever Mike is becoming) lands. Some elements are familiar tropes: wrong-colored eyes, "the fences are just suggestions," taxidermy staring, the humming. The prose occasionally strains—"like a trapped bird," "every evolutionary alarm bell," "cold hit him like a physical blow" are clichés; "burled" for the voice seems an error. Minor mechanical slips (capitalization after "eyes again. tired"), and a slight over-reliance on italicized internal thought. Still, pacing is tight, atmosphere sustained, and the escalation feels motivated rather than arbitrary. The father's transformation is seeded by the clearing scene in the prior chapter, so it reads as earned rather than unearned. Length is approximately on target. Emotionally, fear dominates; complexity comes mainly through JT's shame and filial unease rather than deeper character layers. + Fantasy-humour: Hell is Other Demons — Score: 77.0
Prompt:
Hell is Other Demons Write a day in the life short story. Lucifer morningstar's on again/ off again relationship with Lilith is currently in the "off again" stage, though the cycle may be coming around as Lilith has been stopping by for reasons other than purely violent ones, and Lucifer has been increasingly lonely. Write a day in the life of this power couple, with elements of dark comedy & fantasy. Use understated irony & absurdity by merging the black immorality and everyday business of running hell, against relatable domestic relationship drama. Take cues from Neil Gaiman. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The ash in Hell does not fall like snow. Snow has the decency to melt; the ash simply accumulates, a greasy, gray confetti of burnt petitions and singed hopes that requires constant sweeping. It settles in the crevices of the basalt architecture and ruins the velvet upholstery. Lucifer Morningstar stood on the balcony of the Pandemonium penthouse, sipping an espresso that was hot enough to strip the enamel off a lesser being’s teeth. He wore a silk dressing gown that shimmered with the color of a bruising sky. He was bored. It was a Tuesday, or perhaps a Thursday. Time in the Pit was less a linear progression and more of a thick, stagnant soup. The only metric that mattered was the relationship cycle, and currently, the Lightbringer was single. "Sir," said Mazikeen, stepping out of the shadows with a clipboard. She looked put out, mostly because she wasn't currently stabbing anyone. "The Soul Processing Union is threatening a strike. They want better dental." "They’re demons, Mazikeen," Lucifer sighed, flicking a speck of ash from his rim. "Their teeth are supposed to be jagged and yellow. It’s part of the aesthetic. Tell them if they strike, I’ll outsource the flaying to the angelic host. They’re terribly efficient, if lacking in artistry." "Noted. Also, she is here." Lucifer didn't need to ask who *she* was. The temperature in the room hadn’t changed, but the air suddenly felt sharper, as if the atoms themselves were holding their breath to avoid being cut. "Send her in. And have the imp sweep the foyer again. It looks like Pompeii out there." Lilith entered not with a bang, but with the confident click-clack of heels that sounded like hammers driving nails into a coffin. She was wearing a business suit cut from the midnight sky, tailored to intimidate. Last month, during the "screaming and throwing molten rock" phase of their breakup, she had tried to eviscerate him with a rib bone. Today, she was carrying a Tupperware container. "Morningstar," she said. Her voice was smoke and old whiskey. "Mother of Demons," Lucifer replied, leaning against the obsidian railing. "To what do I owe the pleasure? I’ve had the locks changed on the armory, if that’s what you’re looking for." "Don't be petty, acts beneath you," Lilith said, placing the container on a table made from the petrified wood of the Tree of Knowledge. "I made too much vindaloo. It’s spicy. Even for down here. I thought you might want it." It was the classic maneuver. The 'Leftover Casserole of Reconciliation.' "How thoughtful," Lucifer said, eyeing the container warily. "Is it poisoned?" "Only emotionally," she said, joining him on the balcony. They stood in silence for a long moment, watching the ash drift down over the sprawling, burning metropolis below. In the distance, the screams of the damned rose in a rhythmic drone, not unlike the sound of heavy traffic on the M25, only slightly more desperate. "The torture pits are looking shabby," Lilith observed, pointing a manicured nail toward the Fourth Circle. "The pitchforks are rusty. And not in the scary, tetanus way. In the lazy, underfunded municipal way." "Budget cuts," Lucifer said defensively. "I’m trying to pivot Hell toward psychological torment. It’s more sustainable. We have a whole department now that just makes people listen to recordings of themselves explaining why they’re 'actually a really nice guy' to their exes." Lilith snorted, a sound that cracked a nearby windowpane. "Soft. You’re going soft, Lucifer. Hell needs viscera. It needs stakes." "I am lonely, Lilith," he said, the words slipping out before he could catch them. He blamed the ash; it clogged the filters of his pride. Lilith didn't look at him. She watched a particularly large winged beast crash into a spire. "I know. I haven't had anyone to properly argue with for weeks. Asmodeus just agrees with me. It’s infuriating. I want to be challenged, not worshipped." "We could argue now, if you like?" Lucifer offered politely. "I could say something distinctive about your management of the Succubus division, and you could threaten to unmake me." "I'm too tired," she admitted, brushing a flake of gray soot from his lapel. The gesture was shockingly intimate, more dangerous than the rib bone had been. "The ash is terrible today." "It’s the new intake from the surface. They have very flammable anxieties." "You should get a dome," she suggested. "Or an umbrella. A very large, black umbrella." "I’ll put it on the agenda." They stood there, two ancient, cosmic entities, vibrating with enough power to shatter stars, awkwardly navigating the minefield of domesticity. The tension was palpable—a taut wire between the Lord of the Damned and the First rebel. "I have some paperwork to file," Lucifer said, lying. "Reviewing the punishment for people who talk on speakerphone in public restrooms." "An eternity of being interrupted?" Lilith guessed. "An eternity of silence where they can hear nothing but their own breathing, amplified to deafening levels. But," he paused, turning to face her. "I could be persuaded to take a break. There is a new vintage of blood wine from the Borgia cellars." Lilith smiled. It was a smile that had toppled kingdoms and convinced Eve to take a bite. It was terrifying. It was lovely. "I suppose I can stay," she said. "But only to critique your upholstery. This velvet is hideous." "It’s the ash," Lucifer protested, leading her back inside, away from the gray drizzle. "I can’t keep it clean." "Then change the fabric, darling," she said, slipping her arm through his. "Leather. Much easier to wipe down. You really are hopeless without me." "Entirely," Lucifer agreed, feeling the cold, hard knot in his chest loosen just a fraction. Outside, the ash continued to fall, coating the damned and the demons alike in the debris of human failure. But inside the penthouse, amidst the complaints about furniture and the looming threat of labor strikes, the fires were burning just a little bit brighter. The cycle was turning. It was, all things considered, a lovely day in the neighborhood.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece delivers exactly what the prompt requested: a day-in-the-life of Lucifer and Lilith in their "off again" phase edging toward reconciliation, with dark comedy, understated irony, and Gaiman-esque domesticity-of-the-cosmic. The ash-as-snow inversion is a strong opening image, and the "Leftover Casserole of Reconciliation" is a genuinely funny, well-observed beat. The dialogue crackles with dry wit ("Only emotionally," "Don't be petty, acts beneath you" — though the latter has a slightly garbled construction). The union strike over dental, the speakerphone punishment, and the upholstery critique all successfully merge infernal bureaucracy with relatable relationship drama. Strengths: consistent ironic tone, economical worldbuilding, believable emotional beats (Lucifer's loneliness slipping out, Lilith's weariness with being worshipped), and a satisfying arc where intimacy returns through small gestures rather than grand declarations. Weaknesses: The piece leans on familiar tropes — Mazikeen with a clipboard, the "smoke and whiskey voice," the penthouse in Pandemonium — that feel borrowed from the TV show Lucifer more than Gaiman. Some jokes are easy (M25 comparison, "lovely day in the neighborhood" closer). Lilith's character is thinner than Lucifer's; her motivations are stated rather than dramatized. The ending is a touch tidy and warm, though the prompt invited the cycle turning, so it's mostly earned. Occasional clichés ("the tension was palpable," "taut wire") betray first-draft phrasing. The prose is competent but rarely transcendent; it's witty rather than beautiful. Overall: a polished, entertaining dark comedy that fulfills the brief with skill, held back from excellence by derivativeness and a few stock phrases. + Historical fiction: Gladiator — Score: 77.5
Prompt:
Historical Fiction: Write a scene from a story set during the height of the Roman Empire, focusing on a slice of a day in the life of a gladiator. Do not write a combat scene. Use sensory details to capture the sights, sounds, and smells of ancient Rome. Explore the gladiator's thoughts and emotions. The story should also touch on the larger political and social issues of the time period. The piece should feel like a slice of a larger story. First person, past tense, 1000 words.
Model Output:
The dust of the *Ludus Magnus* did not taste like the earth of my homeland. In the north, the dirt was rich, dark, and smelled of rain and rotting leaves. Here, in the bowels of Rome, the dust tasted of pulverized stone, dried blood, and the eternal, oppressive heat that radiated from the bricks. I sat on a low wooden bench in the semi-darkness of the holding area, the sounds of the world above filtering down through the grate like the muffled roar of a distant ocean. It was mid-day. The *venationes*—the beast hunts—were finishing. I could hear the rhythmic chanting of fifty thousand citizens, a sound that vibrated in the marrow of my bones. They were screaming for meat. "Listen to them," muttered Galen, a Retiarius from Gaul who sat across from me, picking at a callous on his palm. "They sound hungrier than the lions today." " The grain fleet from Egypt is late," I said, keeping my voice low. "The Emperor knows empty bellies make for rebellion. So, he feeds them blood instead of bread." It was a cynical thought, but Rome was a cynical city. I had been here four years, long enough to understand the mechanics of the Empire better than the free men who cheered for my death. We were the distraction. We were the grease in the gears of the *Pax Romana*. As long as the mob was screaming for Varo the Thracian to sever a jugular, they weren't screaming for the Senate to lower the price of oil. I looked down at my hands. They were wrapped in leather straps, stiff with dried sweat and old oil. Resting across my knees was my *sica*. It was a beautiful, hateful thing. Unlike the straight, efficient *gladius* of the Roman legions—a weapon designed for the disciplined shield wall—the *sica* was curved, angled sharply forward like the talon of a raptor or the tusk of a boar. It was the weapon of the Thraex, the role I had been cast in because of my height and my origin. I ran a thumb along the flat of the blade. It was shorter than a sword but longer than a dagger. Its significance lay in its geometry. When a heavy Roman scutum shield was locked in front of me, an impenetrable wall of wood and bronze, the *sica* was the answer. The curve allowed me to reach around the shield’s rim, to hook into the back, or to drive the point downward over the top edge into the collarbone or helmet. It was a weapon of subversion. It did not meet force with force; it found the angle, the weakness, the way around. It was the only thing in this city that did not demand I submit to Roman straight lines and order. "Do you think the Emperor is here?" Galen asked, looking up at the ceiling as if he could see through the stone. "Trajan is always here when the mood is sour," I replied. "He needs to be seen. He needs them to love him more than they hate their hunger." The heavy iron grate at the end of the corridor rattled open. The smell hit us first—a wave of expensive lavender oil battling the stench of the latrines and the copper tang of the butchery happening in the arena. A Lanista walked in, followed by a man in a toga so white it seemed to glow in the dim torchlight. A Senator, or perhaps a high-ranking equestrian. He held a perfumed cloth to his nose, his eyes scanning us like livestock at an auction. He wasn't looking at our faces; he was looking at our shoulders, our calves, the scars that mapped our history. "This one," the Senator said, pointing a soft finger at me. "The Thraex. Is he fit?" "Varo is the best in the school, dominus," the Lanista said, his voice dripping with an obsequious tone that made my stomach turn. "Fourteen victories. He moves like water." The Senator stepped closer. I did not stand. I stayed seated, polishing the curve of my *sica* with a rag. It was a small rebellion, but it was all I had. "The crowd is restless," the Senator said, more to the Lanista than to me. "The beast hunt was... underwhelming. The lions were lethargic. We need a display of skill. Something to remind the people of Roman virtue overcoming the barbarian threat." I tightened my grip on the handle. *Roman virtue.* That was the narrative. I was the barbarian threat. My opponent would be a Murmillo, heavily armored, carrying the large shield and straight sword of the legionary. The play was always the same: Rome against the Wild. Order against Chaos. Even in our death, we were political theater. "He will fight the new Murmillo from Capua," the Lanista promised. "It will be a good show." The Senator looked at me, his eyes meeting mine for the first time. There was no pity there, only calculation. He was wondering if I would die well enough to save his afternoon from boredom. "Make it last," the Senator said. "Don't kill him too quickly. The people need to feel the struggle." He turned and swept out of the room, the white toga vanishing into the gloom. "Make it last," Galen mocked softly. "Easy for him to say. He's not the one bleeding." I stood up, my joints popping. I felt the weight of the *manica* armor on my right arm and the heavy greaves on my legs. The heat was rising. The air in the tunnel was becoming stifling, thick with the humidity of thousands of breathing, sweating bodies packed into the stone bowl above. "It’s time," the Lanista barked. We moved toward the tunnel entrance. The noise grew louder, transforming from a hum into a physical force that battered against my chest. Trumpets blared—harsh, brassy notes that signaled the end of the executions and the beginning of the gladiatorial combat. I checked the *sica* one last time. The blade was clean. It was my partner, my provider, and likely, eventually, my widow. As we walked through the stone corridor, passing the shrine to Nemesis where men prayed for vengeance or mercy, I thought of the grain ships waiting in the harbor at Ostia. I thought of the Senator’s soft hands. I thought of the lie of Rome—that civilization was built on marble and law, when in truth, it was built on this: a man with a curved sword walking into the light to kill another man so the city wouldn't burn itself down. The gate ahead opened. The light was blinding, a wall of white fire. The roar became deafening, a wall of sound. I stepped forward, not for glory, not for the Emperor, but for the weight of the *sica* in my hand and the breath in my lungs. I stepped into the arena, a barbarian king in a cage of gold, ready to give the empire exactly what it deserved.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece is a competent, professional slice-of-life gladiator scene that fulfills nearly all prompt requirements: first person, past tense, non-combat, sensory detail, interiority, political/social commentary, and a clear sense of a larger story. The historical texture is strong—the Ludus Magnus, the sica vs. gladius distinction, the venationes, Trajan-era references, grain fleet politics—and the central conceit (the curved Thracian blade as subversion against Roman straight lines) is a genuinely nice thematic device. Strengths: the prose is controlled and rhythmic; the Senator's inspection scene is well-observed; the "bread and circuses" cynicism is woven in naturally through dialogue; the sensory palette (dust taste, lavender vs. latrines, muffled roar) is vivid without excess. The small rebellion of not standing is a good character beat. Weaknesses: the piece leans heavily on familiar tropes—the cynical gladiator, the effete soft-handed Senator, "barbarian in a gilded cage." The political commentary (grain fleet, Emperor's need to be loved) is somewhat on-the-nose and delivered via exposition-heavy dialogue. Some lines are over-polished aphorisms ("my partner, my provider, and likely, eventually, my widow") that feel writerly rather than organic. The ending's "give the empire exactly what it deserved" is a bit grandiose and slightly muddled in intent. The dialogue is serviceable but occasionally stilted ("The Emperor knows empty bellies make for rebellion"). Word count is roughly on target. There is mild repetitiveness in the "Rome is a lie" thematic restatements. Overall: a polished, engaging, above-average piece that stops short of distinction due to conventional framing and occasional over-explanation. + Epistolary: The Lighthouse Keeper — Score: 74.5
Prompt:
The Lighthouse Keeper Epistolary Narrative: Write a story told entirely through a series of brief correspondences: telegrams or letters or emails between two characters. The correspondence should span several months or years, and reveal a gradually unfolding plot. Use distinct voices for each character, and include details that provide insight into their personalities and motivations. The story should build to an emotional climax, and the final letter should provide a satisfying resolution. The setting is a lighthouse keeper writing to his mother. He is working class and Scottish. He is struggling with the isolation of his posting. Write naturally and without cliches. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**October 14th, 1924** **Ardmore Point Lighthouse** Dearest Ma, I’ve arrived. The boat ride over was a stomach-churner, waves the size of the kirk roof, but I kept my breakfast down, which is more than I can say for the supplies crate. The tower is a stark thing, Ma. Whitewashed stone sticking out of the black rock like a broken bone. It’s colder here than in town, a damp cold that gets into the wool of your jumper. But the pay is as promised. I’ll send the first packet as soon as the supply boat returns next month. Tell Jamie he’s to keep his head in his books and not be looking for work at the docks yet. I’m doing this so he doesn’t have to. My partner is a man named Silas. He’s got a face like a dried apple and says about three words a day. Mostly "coffee" and "wind." Don’t you worry. I’ve got my books, and I’ve got the view. Your loving son, Ewan *** **November 28th, 1924** Ma, I received your parcel. The fruit cake was a bit dry by the time it got here, but it tasted like home, so I ate every crumb. Even Silas had a piece, though he grumbled it needed whiskey. The work is harder than I thought. It’s not just watching the light. It’s the polishing. Endless brass, Ma. The lens is a monster of glass and prism, and if there’s a single smudge, Silas looks at me like I’ve cursed in church. We wind the weights, trim the wicks, scrub the floors. Then we do it again. It’s the noise that gets you. You’d think it would be quiet, but the sea never stops roaring. It bangs against the foundation until you feel it in your teeth. I’m sleeping poorly. I keep dreaming I’m back in the tenement, hearing you humming while you scrub the steps. Then I wake up and it’s just the wind screaming round the gallery. Love to you and the wee ones. Ewan *** **January 5th, 1925** Dear Ma, Happy New Year. I hope you got the money. It’s dark here. Not just night-time dark. The storms have rolled in off the Atlantic and the sky is a bruised purple all day. We haven’t seen the sun in a fortnight. I found the little thing you hid in the bottom of my kit bag. The silver thimble. I laughed when I saw it, thinking you’d gone daft giving a lad a thimble. But then I tore my good trousers on a crate nail and had to mend them. It’s a bonnie thing. I held it up to the lantern light last night. It’s not smooth, is it? It has that pattern of tiny raised diamonds all around the band, and the rim is bent slightly where you said you dropped it on the hearthstone the day Da died. It smells faintly of lavender and iron. When I put it on my pinky—it’s too small for my thumb—it felt cold, then warm. It felt like your hand on my shoulder. I fixed the trousers. The stitching is ugly as sin, but it holds. Silas has taken to talking to the seagulls. I catch him on the gallery, shouting arguments at them. I’m keeping to myself. I miss the noise of the city. I miss the silence of a church. Here, there is neither. Your son, Ewan *** **March 12th, 1925** Ma, I’m sorry for the short letter last time. My head wasn’t right. The isolation is a strange beast. It eats at you. I found myself staring at the rotation gears for an hour yesterday, just watching the teeth mesh together. Click, turn. Click, turn. I thought about how if I put my hand in there, it would stop. Just to see something change. I didn’t do it. Don’t fret. Silas took a fall three days ago. Slippery stairs. His ankle is the size of a grapefruit. He can’t climb the tower, so I’m doing double shifts. Up and down, up and down. My calves are burning and my eyes sting from the paraffin fumes. He sits in the bunk and groans. I have to cook for him, and you know I can barely boil water without burning the pot. I made a stew out of tinned beef and potatoes that looked like grey sludge. He ate it. He told me I’m a "good lad." First time he’s said anything kind. I look at the thimble on the shelf. It’s the only thing here that isn’t made for survival or warning. It’s just for mending. I think I’m trying to mend myself, Ma. Tell Jamie I’m proud of his marks. Ewan *** **April 20th, 1925** Ma, The supply boat didn’t come. The seas are too high. We’re low on coal. We’re burning the furniture to keep the stove going in the kitchen. I’m cold, Ma. Bone deep. I had a bad turn last night. The fog was thick, a white wall pressing against the glass. The horn was blowing every two minutes—a low, mournful blast that shakes your ribs. I started crying. I don’t know why. I was just sitting there by the lantern, watching the beam cut through the nothingness, and I felt like I was the last man on earth. Like you and the city and the world were just stories I told myself. I took the thimble down. I rubbed my thumb over the bent rim until the skin was raw. I tried to remember your face, but it was fuzzy. I’m scared I’m going to forget how to speak to people. I’m scared I’m going to be like Silas, shouting at birds. Pray for me. Ewan *** **May 15th, 1925** Dearest Ma, The storm broke. It was the worst night of my life. The waves were breaking over the gallery rail, a hundred feet up. The noise was like artillery fire. Around midnight, the rotation mechanism jammed. The weights caught. The light stopped turning. If the light stops, ships die. That’s the rule. Silas couldn’t move. I had to go up. I had to climb into the gear housing. It was dark and slick with oil. I had to force the gears free with a crowbar, while the tower swayed in the wind like a drunkard. I thought the glass was going to shatter and suck me out into the dark. I was screaming, Ma. I was cursing the sea and the light and the money. But then I got it loose. The gears caught. The giant lens began to turn. *Swoosh. Swoosh.* The beam swept out over the water. And in that light, for just a second, I saw a trawler. Tiny, bobbing like a cork, way out in the deep. They were too close to the reef. But when the light hit them, they turned. I saw them turn, Ma. They saw me. I sat on the floor of the lantern room and watched them sail away from the rocks. I held the thimble in my pocket. I didn’t feel lonely then. I felt... necessary. The supply boat came this morning. The sun is out. The sea looks innocent, blue and flat, like it never tried to kill us. Silas is going ashore on the boat. He’s retiring. He shook my hand and gave me his pipe. I’m sending this letter with the boatman, but I’m not on it. I’ve signed on for another six months. They’re sending a new junior keeper. A young lad from Glasgow. I’m not staying because I love it. I’m staying because the money will put Jamie through university, not just school. And because I know I can do it now. The silence doesn’t scare me anymore. I know how to fill it. I’ll be home for Christmas, I promise. Keep the kettle on. Your loving son, Ewan
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong epistolary piece with a confident, consistent working-class Scottish voice. Ewan's letters are rich in period-appropriate texture — paraffin fumes, rotation weights, brass polishing — and the thimble is an excellent recurring motif: a domestic, mending object set against a landscape of warning and survival, which the story explicitly and touchingly thematizes ("It's the only thing here that isn't made for survival or warning"). The gradual psychological deterioration is well-paced across the letters, from bravado to intrusive thoughts (the gear-teeth moment is genuinely chilling and handled with restraint), to the fog breakdown, to the storm climax. Key weakness: the prompt asks for correspondence *between two characters*, but we only ever read Ewan's letters. The mother's voice is entirely absent, so the "distinct voices for each character" requirement is only half-met. This is a meaningful adherence failure, though the one-sided form is executed well enough that it reads as a deliberate choice rather than an oversight. Other criticisms: the climax is somewhat conventional — the jammed mechanism, the storm, the near-wrecked trawler turning away just in time — and the resolution arrives a touch neatly, with Ewan's recovery ("I know how to fill it") asserted rather than fully dramatized. The final letter leans on a few stock phrases ("worst night of my life," "last man on earth," "bone deep"), and Silas's transformation from three-words-a-day curmudgeon to pipe-gifting mentor is a familiar arc. The emotional beats occasionally tell rather than show ("I'm scared I'm going to forget how to speak to people" is fine, but "I think I'm trying to mend myself, Ma" spells out the symbolism the thimble already carried). The ending's positivity is earned by the storm sequence, but the six-month re-enlistment is resolved slightly too briskly. Still, the prose is clean and unpretentious, the imagery vivid without purple excess, and the emotional register — loneliness, filial duty, class aspiration via Jamie's education — is genuinely affecting. The lavender-and-iron detail on the thimble is lovely. It falls short of masterpiece mainly through the missing second voice and some conventional plotting. + First-person unique perspective: Hacker Mindset — Score: 79.3
Prompt:
Hacker Mindset Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a reformed (now) white hat hacker who cannot help but notice exploitable weaknesses in both systems and people they encounter. They habitually look for vulnerabilities and exploit vectors. The narrative takes place during a first date at a restaurant, where they're trying to focus on human connection. It's going surprisingly well due to a discovered shared nerd-fandom (magic the gathering). Things go a little sideways when the date reveals a noticeably insecure phone unlock pattern, which protagonist can't help but comment on. They are then left to negotiate the fallout of this faux pas and attempt to salvage (or perhaps sabotage) the remainder of the date. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The WiFi password is `Tiramisu1`. It’s written in thick, black Sharpie on a piece of masking tape stuck to the espresso machine, visible from three tables away. I clocked it four seconds after we walked in. It’s WPA2, sure, but with a password that weak, I could capture the handshake, crack it offline in under ten minutes, and be sniffing the unencrypted traffic of every diner in here before the appetizers arrive. I could probably pivot to the Point of Sale system—it’s almost certainly on the same VLAN—and comp our meal. *Stop it.* I take a sip of water. *Focus on the girl. Focus on Maya.* She is smiling. This is good. A smile is a positive handshake protocol. It indicates the connection is stable. "I can't believe you run a Dimir mill deck," Maya says, shaking her head, though the amusement in her eyes betrays her feigned disgust. "That is so... mean. You’re one of *those* players." "I like win conditions that don't rely on combat damage," I say, leaning in. "It’s about resource denial. Controlling the board state." "It’s about making sure no one else gets to have fun," she counters, laughing. We’re ten minutes in, and the social engineering—no, *socializing*, damn it—is going shockingly well. I usually treat dates like penetration tests: probing for defenses, analyzing responses, waiting for the inevitable rejection packet. But Maya is different. She’s fluent in nerd. Discovering she plays *Magic: The Gathering* was like finding a backdoor into a root shell I didn’t think I had access to. But the noise in my head won't stop. My eyes flick over her shoulder to the waiter punching an order into a terminal. He’s typing with two fingers. I catch the PIN code. `1-4-7-2`. I don't want to know it. I just do. It’s a geometry thing; the shape of his hand movement maps to the keypad layout. If I ever needed to authorize a refund on a steak, I have the credentials. *Look at her eyes. Not the waiter. Not the security camera that has a blind spot in the back corner. Her eyes.* "So," Maya says, "what do you do? You said 'consultant' on your profile, which is usually code for 'unemployed' or 'CIA'." "Cybersecurity," I say. "I break things so people can fix them. White hat. Mostly." "Mostly?" "I used to be... gray. Maybe a dark shade of gray. Now I’m corporate. I get paid to tell banks their vaults are unlocked." She seems intrigued rather than alarmed. This is a critical juncture. Usually, when people hear 'hacker,' they think I’m going to steal their identity. Which I could. But I won't. "That sounds stressful," she says. "Do you ever turn it off?" "I'm trying," I admit. "Right now, for instance. I am trying very hard to just eat this breadstick." She laughs again. The sound is nice. Analog. Uncompressed. Her phone buzzes on the table between us. The screen lights up—a notification from Instagram. She reaches for it instinctively. My brain switches modes instantly. Threat assessment. Observation. She holds the phone in her left hand. Her right index finger hovers. She draws the pattern. Top-left node. Straight down to bottom-left. Straight right to bottom-right. An 'L'. The pattern is an 'L'. It is the default unlock pattern for roughly 15% of Android users. It corresponds to the movement of a knight in chess, but without the strategy. It is the security equivalent of leaving your house key under the doormat, except the doormat is made of glass and says "KEY HERE." The friction in my brain becomes unbearable. It’s like seeing a syntax error in compiling code. It’s a jagged edge. A loose wire. I physically wince. "Is everything okay?" Maya asks, noticing my grimace. She hasn't put the phone down yet. *Don't say it. Do not say it. Just ask about her job. Ask about her cat. Ask about anything else.* "You use an 'L' pattern," I say. The words bypass my firewall completely. Maya freezes. Her thumb hovers over the screen. "What?" "Your unlock pattern," I continue, the verbal diarrhea of a compelled mind spilling out. "Top-left, bottom-left, bottom-right. It’s the most statistically common pattern. It has barely any entropy. If someone stole your phone, that’s the first thing they’d try. Actually, looking at the smudge marks on your screen, I wouldn't even have to guess. The oleophobic coating is worn down in that exact shape. It’s practically a neon sign." Silence. The ambient noise of the restaurant seems to drop away, leaving only the high-pitched whine of my own regret. Maya pulls the phone closer to her chest. Her body language shifts. Shoulders up, chin down. Defensive posture. The firewall is back up. "Did you just... watch me enter my password?" she asks. Her voice isn't angry yet, but it’s cold. "I didn't mean to," I stammer, realizing I’m currently failing the social protocol. "I just noticed. It’s what I do. I see vulnerabilities. It’s a reflex. Like... like how a musician notices when a guitar is out of tune." "So you’re analyzing me?" "No! Well, yes. But not maliciously. I’m analyzing the *system*. You’re just the user." *Terrible phrasing. Abort. Abort.* "I’m not a system," she says, sliding her phone into her purse. The purse zips shut. A physical air-gap. "That’s really creepy." "I know," I say, dropping my head into my hands. "I know it is. I’m sorry. It’s a curse. I walked in here and I saw the WiFi password, the waiter's PIN, and the fact that the manager is running Windows 7 on the back office PC which went end-of-life years ago. I can't help it. My brain is constantly running vulnerability scans." I look up at her. I need to salvage this. I need to patch the exploit I just created in our interaction. "I like you," I say, stripping away the jargon. "I really like that you play a mill deck. I’m trying to be a person, but sometimes the professional paranoia leaks out. I promise I am not trying to hack you. If I were, I wouldn't have told you your security was bad. I would have just waited until you went to the bathroom and cloned your SIM card." Her eyes widen. *Why did I say that? Why is my internal monologue running on a loudspeaker?* "That was a joke," I add quickly. "A bad, specific, technical joke." Maya stares at me for a long five seconds. I calculate the probability of her standing up and leaving. It’s hovering around 60%. Then, she exhales. She reaches into her purse and pulls the phone back out. She holds it under the table, taps on it for a moment, and then puts it back on the tablecloth. "I changed it," she says. "And I wiped the screen on my napkin." I blink. "You did?" "Yes. But if you guess the new one, I’m leaving, and you’re paying for the drinks." "I won't look," I promise. "I’ll look at the ceiling." "Good." She picks up her menu. "And for the record, if you ever tell me my passwords are weak again, you have to fix them for me. Free of charge." "That’s... reasonable," I say, feeling the tension bleed out of my shoulders. "Okay then." She glances over my shoulder. "Now, since you’re so observant... that guy at the bar. The one in the blue shirt." I don't need to turn around. I’ve been tracking him peripherally since he sat down. "The one with the laptop?" "Yeah. Is he hacking the WiFi?" "No," I say. "He’s torrenting movies. He’s using a public tracker without a VPN. If the ISP checks the logs, the restaurant is going to get a copyright strike letter in about three days." Maya smiles. It’s a genuine smile again. The handshake is re-established. "Okay," she says. "That’s actually kind of cool. Like a superpower. A really nerdy, socially awkward superpower." "I'll take it," I say. I pick up the menu. I try to focus on the appetizers. But in the back of my mind, a background process is still running. I’m still watching the waiter. I’m still clocking the camera angles. I’m still thinking about how easy it would be to secure her phone with a proper biometric lock. But for now, I keep my mouth shut. I’ve successfully mitigated the threat. The system is stable. "So," I say. "Dimir. Tell me about your mana curve."
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece executes the brief with impressive precision. The first-person internal monologue is sustained throughout, with the hacker's compulsive threat-assessment running as a "background process" that constantly intrudes on the date. The technical voice is authentic and consistent—WiFi handshakes, VLAN pivots, PIN observation via hand geometry, smudge-pattern analysis on the oleophobic coating—all of it is plausible, specific, and character-revealing rather than decorative. The MTG detail is well-deployed: the Dimir mill deck is a cleverly apt choice (the guild literally themed around espionage, surveillance, and mind-reading), and the banter about resource denial versus fun establishes genuine rapport before the inciting incident. The "L" pattern observation is handled well—the protagonist's wince, the failed self-censorship ("the words bypass my firewall completely"), and the escalating verbal missteps feel true to the character. The recovery arc is the piece's strongest and weakest element. Maya's response—changing the pattern, wiping the screen, issuing a playful ultimatum—is a satisfying turn that rewards the protagonist's honesty, and her pivot to asking about the bar guy's laptop cleverly reframes his "curse" as a shared game. However, the forgiveness arrives a touch quickly and conveniently; a real person might reasonably walk out after the SIM-cloning "joke," and the piece smooths that over slightly. The ending's return to "Tell me about your mana curve" is a nice callback that closes the loop without over-sentimentalizing. Minor flaws: some metaphors are stock hacker-cliché ("firewall," "handshake protocol," "background process") though they're at least diegetic to the character's worldview; the "analog, uncompressed" laugh is a bit precious; and the prose occasionally tells us the emotional stakes ("I need to patch the exploit I just created") rather than letting them land. The waiter PIN and Windows 7 asides are efficient worldbuilding. Prose is clean, rhythmic, and controlled, with good comic timing in the dialogue.
